deep.reconstruction:
Context: this sheet sits between an envelope addressed to Gauss, which shows a tilted square drawn on a 3×3 dot lattice, and a page on least residues modulo a Gaussian integer a+ib, with an index table modulo −7+10i. So it belongs to Gauss's work on biquadratic residues in Z[i].

(1) Data. The left column reads A=−3, B=+2, norm 13 and a=+1, b=+2, norm 5. So two Gaussian primes are being compared: m=a+bi=1+2i (N=5) and M=A+Bi=−3+2i (N=13). The third line reads α=+1, β=−8. These are α=aA+bB=1 and β=bA−aB=−8, i.e. α+βi=(a+bi)(A−Bi)=(1+2i)(−3−2i)=1−8i. The number β=−8 is the determinant of the linear map used below.

(2) The map. Let z=ξ+iη be a point of the plane. Gauss sets
 x+iy=(1+2i)z and X+iY=(−3+2i)z,
which gives
 x=ξ−2η, y=2ξ+η, X=−3ξ−2η, Y=2ξ−3η.
Only the formulas for X and x are written on the page; the expressions for y and Y are my completion, forced by the later lines. Points of the plane thus carry two coordinate systems: the grid of (1+2i)z and the grid of (−3+2i)z. The pencil sketches show two tilted squares (fundamental domains of the moduli) superposed on a square grid, with the overlap divided into regions labelled 0, 1, 2, 3; a small ink copy of the labelled square also appears. The computations find the vertices of these regions as intersections of grid lines of the two systems.

(3) Vertex with X=−1, x=−1/2. Eliminating ξ and η gives 8Y=13x−X, written by Gauss as −8Y=+13/2−1. Hence Y=−11/16 (not written out). Also ξ=(x−X)/4=1/8 and η=−(3x+X)/8=5/16.

(4) Vertex with X=−1, y=1/2. Here the inverse map has determinant 1: ξ=X+2y and η=−2X−3y. Hence x=5X+8y=4−5=−1 and Y=8X+13y=13/2−8=−3/2. Both values are written on the page (the last one truncated as "−"). Here z=i/2.

(5) Vertex with y=1, Y=−1. Solving y=2ξ+η and Y=2ξ−3η (determinant −8) gives:
 −8ξ=−3y−Y, so ξ=1/4;
 −8η=−2y+2Y, so η=1/2;
 −8x=y−5Y, so x=−3/4;
 −8X=13y−Y, so X=−7/4.
Check: z=¼+½i=¼(1+2i). Then (1+2i)z=¼(1+2i)²=−3/4+i, which reproduces x=−3/4, y=1. And (−3+2i)z=¼(1+2i)(−3+2i)=¼(−7−4i)=−7/4−i, which reproduces X=−7/4, Y=−1. This is the line "¼+½i … ¼(1+2i)(−3+2i)" with "−7/4−i" beneath it.

(6) Unclear jottings. The fragments "−2i −0i / −1" and the right-hand table of pairs (−1+0, −1+2, +2−3, −1+0 | −0+1, +3+1, +2+2, −1, +1) appear to list lattice points or residues and their coordinates for the region count. I cannot reconstruct them with certainty.

Purpose (interpretation, not certain): a geometric, lattice-point study of how a residue system modulo one Gaussian prime lies relative to the other prime's fundamental square, split into quadrant classes 0–3. This is a biquadratic analogue of the Gauss-lemma / lattice-point approach to reciprocity, worked on the smallest example 1+2i, −3+2i.
errors: No arithmetic errors found in the readable computations.
The line '¼+½i = ¼(1+2i)(−3+2i)' is not a literal equality. It is shorthand: z=¼+½i=¼(1+2i), and multiplying by (−3+2i) gives −7/4−i, written below.
In the X=−1, x=−½ case, Gauss stops at −8Y=13/2−1 and does not write the value Y=−11/16.

results.what: Expressing a plane point z simultaneously in the coordinate systems (1+2i)z and (−3+2i)z, and solving for intersections of grid lines. The determinant is bA−aB=−8 and the cross product is (a+bi)(A−Bi)=1−8i.
results.modern_name: Linear change of lattice coordinates; superposition of fundamental domains of two Gaussian-integer lattices
results.usually_credited_to: Lattice-point methods for reciprocity: Eisenstein (1844, quadratic case); Gauss's lemma for quartic residues treated by Gauss/Eisenstein

results.what: Geometric partition of the overlap of the two tilted squares into regions labelled 0–3 (quadrant classes), apparently toward a biquadratic Gauss-lemma / lattice-count argument
results.modern_name: Gauss's lemma for the quartic residue symbol / lattice-point proof attempt of biquadratic reciprocity
results.usually_credited_to: Eisenstein (1844) for published proofs of biquadratic reciprocity; Gauss stated the law (1832) and claimed a proof

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's unpublished work toward biquadratic reciprocity and least residues mod a+bi is known from the Nachlass. A geometric lattice-region approach with explicit vertex computations is a notable but fragmentary detail. It cannot be shown here to amount to a complete proof.

checkable.asserts: x+iy=(1+2i)z gives x=-3/4, y=1 at z=1/4+i/2
x=5X+8y and Y=8X+13y, so X=-1, y=1/2 gives x=-1, Y=-3/2

transcription_corrections: 'y = i [?]' should read y = ½ (case X=−1, y=½).
'Y = 13/2 − 8 = −' is truncated; the intended value is −3/2.
Line 1 under the data heading: the entries are (A=−3, B=+2, norm 13) and (a=+1, b=+2, norm 5); α=+1, β=−8 are aA+bB and bA−aB.
'¼+½i = i/4(1+2i)(−3+2i)' should be read as z=¼+½i=¼(1+2i), times (−3+2i) giving −7/4−i; the factor is ¼, not i/4.
